title: A Guide to Healthy Eating

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: James Wong is a London ethnobotanist whose focus is on plants and how we use them. The inspiration for his new book, How to Eat Better, came while he was in Japan. One day he happened to meet a woman whose job was to advise people on the selection, storage and preparation, and nutritional value of produce. Some high-end restaurants and hotels hire such people to collaborate on menus. Intrigued, he took a closer look at the science of produce to find out if we could increase the benefits we get from everyday foods. He spent two years poring over every piece of research he could lay his hands on.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: ‘I really object to the notion that food must be expensive to be good for you,’ says Wong. He argues that not everything sold in a can is bad for our health. Canned tomatoes are an example of this. The cooking and processing of tomatoes increases the amount of lycopene that the body is able to absorb from them. This antioxidant is believed to be beneficial in preventing illnesses such as some cancers and lowering the risk of stroke. It’s also nice to know that tinned tomatoes are just as good as raw ones, because they are affordable and convenient.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: ‘Most people think of fruit and veg as not living,’ says Wong. They assume that once you’ve picked it, nothing is going to change. But in the fruit and vegetable aisle, they’re still living plants. So, ‘wounding’ your vegetables – slicing cabbage into a slaw, grating carrots – stimulates their pest-fighting response and sends levels of beneficial compounds soaring. Some vegetables, leafy greens such as spinach for example, are best consumed immediately after harvest or with minimum delay. If you store mushrooms in a sunny spot in your garden for a couple of hours, their vitamin D levels will rocket because they have a very similar reaction to the one that happens in human skin when exposed to sunlight. Winter squash contains high levels of fibre, potassium and vitamin C, and studies have indicated that people suffer fewer issues with their eyes if they consume them regularly. Pumpkin improves immunity against everyday illnesses such as colds. There may be evidence to suggest that a substance called carotene, found in some vegetables like carrots, is good for the respiratory system. For this reason, since carotene is particularly high in the skin of vegetables, this should be consumed rather than thrown away.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Another problem is the practice of using the word ‘processed’ as a byword for bad. ‘In many instances, processing is wonderful. Chewing is a process, cooking is a process,’ according to Wong. Processed beetroot, pre-cooked and vacuum packed, has been shown to have not only more antioxidant capacity than raw beetroot, but also potentially more healthy betalains – the pigments that make the flesh red – than home-cooked beets. But still some people are sceptical. Wong also discusses the popular notion that modern, high-yield varieties and over-cultivated soils result in crops that are less nutritious. There is some good research coming out of the US that indicates this may be the case for some nutrients – but not all and not all crops. ‘The upside is that modern agriculture has increased productivity, so fruit and vegetables are much cheaper and we’re able to eat more of them,’ says Wong.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Wong is not against fresh food – his new book is full of simple, healthy ways to prepare it – but he isn’t fond of the extremism that goes along with healthy eating. Science and good sense go hand-in-hand for Wong, which is why he’s finding healthy ways to put carbohydrates back on the menu. Cutting them out is impractical for people’s budgets and they are also extremely ecofriendly. He points out that carbs, such as rice and potatoes, create the largest number of calories per square metre of land or per unit of water. Red and black varieties of rice also pack in more polyphenols – another group of beneficial chemicals – than blueberries, which are marketed as a food superstar. And don’t give up on potatoes. Go for small ones that have more phytonutrients (eat the skin), and less effect on blood sugar.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Wong’s final point is all about appearance. In general, purple and red are the shades to be looking for in plant foods: purple carrots rather than orange; purple sweet potato or cauliflower instead of white; red capsicum not green; dark-red Morello cherries rather than those pretty yellow ones. The same goes for apples – Braeburn and Red Delicious outrank Granny Smiths. If you follow his advice, there will be pay-offs, such as slowing the memory decline that some people experience in their later years. Not that he’s expecting you to remember every one of his antioxidant-rich pieces of information. ‘The more tips you follow, the more benefit you’ll get,’ he says. ‘But at the end of the day, the healthiest vegetable is the one you are likeliest to eat.’
